why: B swaps in a new framework and adds a meta line about mapping; A keeps the accurate four-risk frame, though both are wordy.
Much shorter, keeps the core point and drops the anxiety narration and the 'used to think' preamble.
The guess prompt comes before the reveal; B puts the reveal first and then asks for a guess.
Shorter; B's added 'shape the rules together' line is low-value.
The added clause says what to do with the check, and 'possible problem' is a plain, accurate claim.
'Session' is the plainer, student-recognisable word. A's 'run' is jargon.
The title states the point, and it avoids B's repeated line before 'Taste closes the gap'.
Shorter; B's added M6 aside and flywheel kicker are clever extras.
Cuts the course-referential clause 'the shape the whole map has had from the start'.
B's closing line is a slogan after the point.
'Exercise' is the course's proper term for what was run; B's 'prompts' is vaguer.
'Scrollback' is the plainer term and the sentence is tighter.
B's forward hint about Module 4 is low value; A is shorter.
'YOUR real work is the material' opens on the point and is plainer.
B adds a restating sentence; A is shorter.
B ends on a forward hint about later phases; cut it.
B drops a sentence narrating the test steps; same point, fewer words.
'It often isn't. It's a draft' is the more precise claim than 'often just a draft'.
B cuts the sentence about the course's own labelling and what you are not learning.
B adds a redundant sentence that conflicts with the later 'try in your own session'.
A uses a frame without a count; the number does no memory work.
B drops the count from the title, which does no memory work.
B's title is concrete and says what the slide shows; A's is vaguer.
A names the concrete mechanism (MCP tools landing in the same set); B's 'what it leaves out' is vague.
B's added line is a congratulating, narrator-style sentence; shorter A wins.
B is tighter, plainer, and reads faster than A's long clause-heavy list, though it adds a couple of sentences.
B's opener is a low-value orienting sentence; cut it.
B adds a redundant lead clause that the next sentence already makes.
'Check' is arguably imprecise but 'read' implies reading everything; the author prefers spot-check, and B moves away from 'read'.
B's forest/trees idiom is a clever kicker; A states the point plainly.
A's shorter header states the action; B's header is longer without adding information.
Names the actor, 'The LLM answers in essays', a concrete subject and the author's own example.
Author kept the 'Oldskool: ccstatusline or /statusline' wording as the recommended advanced option.
A's ADR line is plain and literal; B's 'a future engineer can inspect' adds words.
'The wall' is a made-up concept the author rejected; B drops it.
A's header is concrete and pictureable and the paragraph earns it; B's header is an abstract claim restated by the body.
Shorter header; 'window' is clear from the body.
The extra line is a clever kicker after the point already made.
Drops the count, so no number doing no memory work.
Names the action directly instead of previewing the prompt.
The closing line is a useful clarification, and B drops it for no gain.
Keeps the permission line 'you don't need to get it right first time'.
Concrete action the student takes, in few words; B is abstract and wordy.
Cuts the orientation and connective sentences about the course itself.
'Alternatives' is plainer than 'committed changes'; also avoids the extra 'gives you the floor' clause.
